title: Organised Crime Bill violates rights standards: HRW | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 2 November 2026 03:34
-     - 14

Repealing the PTA would fulfill a key commitment that Sri Lanka made to the European Union, in exchange for tariff-free access to the EU market under its Generalised Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+) program. However, the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill preserves the terrorism act’s abusive features, further weakening Sri Lanka’s compliance with its GSP+ human rights commitments

The Sri Lankan Government’s Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, submitted to Parliament on 20 October, 2026, risks enabling arbitrary detention, torture, and other rights violations, Human Rights Watch said. The proposed law, alongside the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill submitted on 6 October, reproduces abusive provisions in existing counterterrorism laws that would allow continuing abuses that the Government had pledged to end.

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s National People’s Power alliance pledged in its 2024 election manifesto to abolish all “oppressive” laws and ensure “civil rights of people in all parts of the country.” In particular, the Dissanayake Government—like its predecessors—pledged to repeal the notorious Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA). Both bills presented in October replicate some of the worst aspects of the PTA, shifting abusive provisions to create parallel legal structures outside existing criminal law and without basic safeguards.

Human Rights Watch Asia Director Elaine Pearson said: “Sri Lanka’s organised crime bill would enable prolonged detention without adequate judicial oversight or evidence of criminal conduct, and could encourage torture by allowing convictions based on confessions obtained by the Police. If this law is adopted in its current form, it risks unleashing serious rights violations just as previous similarly draconian legislation has done.”

The purported objectives of the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill are to combat organised crime and support international law enforcement cooperation. It is presented as giving effect to the 2003 United Nations Convention against Transnational Organised Crime, yet fails to adhere to international standards of precision and legal certainty and removes basic due process safeguards provided in ordinary Sri Lankan criminal law, enabling the authorities to use arbitrary powers in a wide range of ill-defined circumstances.

The bill defines “serious crime” as any offense punishable with at least four years in prison and lists a large number of offenses that fall under other laws, placing a wide variety of alleged criminal activity within its extraordinary authority. It defines an “organised criminal group” as three or more people acting in concert with the aim of committing one or more serious crimes to obtain, directly or indirectly, a financial or other material benefit.

Courts may consider whether a person is a member of an organised criminal group based on factors including physical or virtual meetings with known members; their style of dress, hand signs, language or tattoos; association with known members of the group; and habitually visiting premises known to be used by the group. Such provisions risk criminalising association rather than conduct, allowing the authorities to detain a person without any evidence of criminal activity.

The bill would allow the Public Security Ministry Secretary  to issue a detention order for two months at a time, for up to a year, without giving the magistrate discretion to set the detention order aside. Bail may be granted only by the High Court, with suspects accused of a serious crime only released on bail in exceptional circumstances.

In the past, the PTA incentivised torture by allowing convictions based on confessions obtained by the police. Recent reform attempts including the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill required instead for confessions to be made to a magistrate. Nevertheless, the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill reproduces the abusive practice of making confessions to the police admissible in court, incentivising coercion, ill-treatment, and torture.

The bill provides police with broad surveillance authority, including to intercept and record communications, carry out forensic extraction of data from electronic devices, and access data from telecommunications companies and online services, through court orders.

The Government did not appear to conduct consultations while drafting the bill. The Government should withdraw the bill, undertake a genuine, open, and inclusive consultation, ensure legislation with robust safeguards to prevent arbitrary detention, torture, and ill treatment, and ensure judicial oversight and due process, in compliance with the Government’s international legal obligations

The Police could, even without a Courtorder, obtain any telecommunication, satellite, or digital service provider information relating to the identity of the owner or subscriber, calls, and the tower location, of any device, sweeping powers to expose personal communications and information and infringe rights, including of privacy and assembly. Sri Lankan law enforcement and security agencies have a long record of misusing surveillance to target human rights defenders and the families of victims of rights violations.

The organised crime bill also contains sections that could curtail freedom of expression by making it an offense to publish the name or anything that could identify a victim of crime. Further restrictions are placed on media reporting of court proceedings without court permission.

The bill also gives the Police broad powers, on “reasonable suspicion” of a serious crime, to stop and search individuals and vehicles, or make arrests and seize relevant items. They could enter and search premises without a warrant. Taken together, the additional Police powers with little or no judicial oversight are wide open to abuse, Human Rights Watch said. Sri Lanka’s experience with the PTA demonstrates the potential for serious rights violations under the Organised Crimes Bill.

Repealing the PTA would fulfill a key commitment that Sri Lanka made to the European Union, in exchange for tariff-free access to the EU market under its Generalised Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+) program. However, the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill preserves the terrorism act’s abusive features, further weakening Sri Lanka’s compliance with its GSP+ human rights commitments.

The Government did not appear to conduct consultations, while drafting the bill. The Government should withdraw the bill, undertake a genuine, open, and inclusive consultation, ensure legislation with robust safeguards to prevent arbitrary detention, torture, and ill treatment, and ensure judicial oversight and due process, in compliance with the Government’s international legal obligations.

“Every Government has a duty to combat organised crime, but needs to do so in compliance with international human rights standards,” Pearson said. “The European Union should make it clear that this bill would not meet Sri Lanka’s obligations under the GSP+ trade program.”

title: Bird’s-eye view: Economy stable and growing. Worm’s-eye view: Not so rosy | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 2 November 2026 03:20
-     - 23

The private sector, widely regarded as the engine of growth in Sri Lanka, contributes more than three-quarters of the country’s national wealth. Yet,  unresolved governance failures in some businesses leave workers and consumers vulnerable. Two examples illustrate the problem: the exploitation of young workers by small garment factories operating outside Colombo, and the defrauding of customers by corrupt insurance agents

Multilateral lenders such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank continue to commend Sri Lanka’s recovery from the devastating crisis of 2022. From their macroeconomic—or bird’s-eye—view, the picture looks encouraging. Budgetary numbers are improving, reforms are progressing, inflation remains in single digits despite recently exceeding the Central Bank’s upper limit, foreign reserves are rising, and economic growth of 5% suggests a firm recovery. To international donors and local policymakers, the message is reassuring: the economy is stable and growing.

Lower the gaze to the ground, however, and the worm’s-eye view is strikingly different. Macroeconomic indicators cannot capture the hardships endured by ordinary people. Economics is not merely about aggregates; it is about human lives. Seen from above, a tree may display a flourishing green canopy. Examined leaf by leaf, it may reveal diseases quietly consuming it.

This problem is not new. In ancient Lanka, courtiers often assured kings that their subjects were content while concealing their hardships. Wise rulers therefore travelled through villages at night in disguise, discovering conditions for themselves and addressing grievances before they threatened the realm.

Ignoring today’s ground reality carries a similarly heavy price. People burdened by silent discontent become easy prey for opportunistic politicians, fraudulent operators, and pyramid schemes that exploit financial distress. The Government cannot afford to disregard this danger.

Looking at typical ground-level cases

Macroeconomic data alone cannot reveal conditions at ground level. A close examination of cases involving frustrated citizens shows discontent that official statistics rarely capture but that dominates the daily lives of many families.

Three broad causes recur: corrupt private-sector practices that cheat consumers and workers; public-sector failures that subject citizens to needless hardship; and banking rigidities that drive vulnerable borrowers into the hands of loan sharks.

Because these grievances are seldom assembled into formal macroeconomic assessments, they often fail to reach policymakers. The result is a dangerous disconnect between reassuring economic indicators at the top and painful realities at the bottom.

Poor governance in private sector

The private sector, widely regarded as the engine of growth in Sri Lanka, contributes more than three-quarters of the country’s national wealth. Yet, 

 unresolved governance failures in some businesses leave workers and consumers vulnerable. Two examples illustrate the problem: the exploitation of young workers by small garment factories operating outside Colombo, and the defrauding of customers by corrupt insurance agents.

In the first case, a young woman—call her Janet—is recruited as a new employee by an outstation garment factory. Her letter of appointment promises a fixed salary and a monthly incentive if she meets her production targets. At the end of her first month, however, no wages are credited to her bank account. When she asks why, she is told that a computer-system failure caused the delay and that payment will be made once the system is restored. The same thing happens at the end of the second month. Unable to endure the situation, Janet complains to the head office, where an officer informally tells her that such non-payment is common at the factory. She later learns that the managers have been withholding the wages of new recruits and pressuring them to leave before the practice is exposed. Following her complaint, Janet receives part of her back pay, but she resigns because she can no longer work under managers whose misconduct she has reported. The managers thus achieve their apparent objective: forcing another new employee to leave. Because they consistently meet their production targets, the head office has also turned a blind eye to their corrupt practices.

The second case concerns corrupt insurance agents at major insurance companies who exploit the three-month credit window available when arranging a policy. This practice is particularly common in motor-vehicle insurance. A vehicle owner pays the premium to an agent, but instead of remitting it to the insurer, the agent pockets the money. The agent then issues documentation that appears to provide cover for a full year, although the policy is valid for only three months. The fraud usually comes to light only after the vehicle is involved in an accident and the owner submits a claim. By then, the policy has lapsed. Although insurance companies may be aware of this misconduct, they sometimes fail to act because the offenders are high-performing “golden agents”.

These cases demonstrate how poor governance can persist in both small and large private businesses. In each instance, commercial success shields misconduct, while workers and customers bear the cost. Such abuses may remain invisible in national accounts, but at ground level they cause severe financial and personal hardship.

Silent suffering of silvering people

Senior citizens—many now visibly silver-haired—are another group suffering silently at ground level. Their number, estimated at 3.92 million, or about 18% of the population, continues to grow. Traditional family support has weakened as children migrate abroad or, even when living in Sri Lanka, struggle with pressures of their own families and workplaces. Many older people must therefore rely largely on savings accumulated during their working lives. Yet the interest income on which they depend is subject to taxation of up to 36%, substantially reducing their disposable income. When they spend what remains on daily necessities and medical care, it is eroded further by indirect taxes and the high cost of living. Government support is limited, while pensions and other fixed incomes do not rise in step with the Central Bank’s inflation target of 5%, with an upper limit of 7%—a limit that can be breached when external shocks strike. It is reported that even the Central Bank’s own retirees, once among the country’s more secure pensioners, now feel these pressures. Their experience illustrates the article’s central contrast: a recovery that appears stable from the bird’s-eye view may still leave many senior citizens facing severe insecurity at the worm’s-eye level.

Government failures or inefficiencies

In some areas, the Government sector performs remarkably well. Sri Lanka Customs and the Inland Revenue Department, for example, have met revenue targets assigned by the budget, demonstrating that public institutions can deliver when goals, systems, and accountability are clear. Elsewhere, however, failures and inefficiencies cause immense hardship. Sri Lanka is rightly proud of maintaining free healthcare and education for decades. These services have expanded opportunity and social welfare, yet weaknesses in their day-to-day delivery provoke widespread public outcry. Citizens value the principle of universal provision but suffer when the institutions established to honour that principle cannot provide timely, dependable service.

In Government hospitals, shortages of basic facilities leave patients distressed. A patient may receive an appointment for critical surgery, make the necessary family and financial arrangements, and enter a major hospital expecting treatment. Only after admission may the operation be postponed because a surgeon, essential medicine, or vital machine is unavailable. The delay is not merely administrative: it prolongs illness, increases uncertainty, and may impose additional travel and living costs on the family. Wards are frequently overcrowded, beds are scarce, and some patients remain standing for hours while waiting for attention. Doctors, nurses, and other staff may work under severe pressure, but the citizen experiences the institution as a whole. A service intended to protect people at their most vulnerable can therefore add pain and uncertainty.

Schools suffer similar weaknesses. Students often complain that teaching in mathematics, information technology, and physics is difficult to understand during normal classroom hours. Because success at national examinations shapes access to higher education and employment, parents cannot simply wait for the system to improve. They purchase private tuition, sometimes through costly home visits by the same teachers responsible for those subjects at school. In effect, the principal learning support shifts from the publicly funded classroom to a private transaction. Such tuition can absorb nearly half the monthly income of a typical middle-class family, forcing sacrifices in food, healthcare, savings, and other essentials. Families thus finance free education through taxes and then pay again for the instruction their children need. The burden is even harsher for poor households that cannot afford supplementary teaching at all.

Administrative delays compound the burden. Vehicle owners may wait 15 months after registration for official number plates, despite having completed the required procedures and payments. Until the plates arrive, they face uncertainty in using or transferring their vehicles. Drivers who pass the prescribed tests may likewise fail to receive permanent licences because cards are unavailable. Temporary arrangements do not remove the inconvenience or anxiety caused by the State’s inability to issue a basic document. These may seem minor problems from above, but at ground level they consume time, disrupt daily life, and expose law-abiding citizens to needless uncertainty.

The police are also criticised for failing to pursue petty robbers and those engaged in roadside intimidation. Drug addicts seeking easy money sometimes stage minor accidents involving elderly or female motorists and then demand payment, relying on fear and confusion to secure a quick settlement. Victims may provide motorcycle registration numbers or photographs of alleged offenders, yet their complaints can meet with inaction. To an institution dealing with grave crimes, each incident may appear small. To the victim, however, it is a direct threat to personal safety and confidence in the law. Repeated inaction signals to offenders that vulnerable road users are easy targets. Such failures erode trust in law enforcement and deepen the sense that ordinary citizens must protect themselves.

These failures inflict pain that aggregate statistics cannot measure. Citizens judge the State by whether a hospital performs a scheduled operation, a school teaches effectively, a department issues an essential document promptly, and the police respond when help is sought. When basic services fail, the worm’s-eye view remains far less reassuring than the bird’s-eye view.

Underhand payments to petrol-pump operators

Even well-intentioned regulations can backfire when they ignore behaviour at ground level. Sri Lanka introduced a Quick Response (QR) code to ration petrol and diesel during a period of scarcity, limiting most motorcars to 25 litres a week. An odd-and-even date rule tied eligibility to registration numbers and was intended to control queues and distribute limited supplies fairly. Yet many motorists found the quota inadequate for commuting and essential travel. The date restriction created a further difficulty: an empty tank on the wrong day could leave a driver stranded even when fuel was available. A rule designed at the centre for orderly allocation thus created powerful incentives for evasion at the pump.

The system consequently gave fuel-pump operators power to profit from desperation. A motorist facing urgent travel could make an underhand cash payment, after which the restrictions suddenly became flexible. An operator who controlled access to the pump could manipulate the process and dispense fuel beyond the weekly quota, even on an ineligible day. Compliance therefore depended not only on technology but also on the integrity of those implementing it. When implementation is weak, a digital rule can merely shift discretion—and the opportunity for corruption—to another level.

A mechanism intended to ensure equity thus bred ground-level corruption. Money that should have entered the revenues of State or private petroleum companies flowed instead into individual pockets. Honest motorists either accepted inadequate supplies or paid bribes to overcome the restrictions, while those with connections or cash obtained more. Ordinary citizens were pushed towards misconduct merely to meet transport needs, widening the gap between clean digital models and compromised daily reality.

Taken together, these ground-level realities reveal a fractured recovery. The bird’s-eye view of lenders and policymakers shows fiscal discipline, single-digit inflation, rising reserves, and renewed growth. The worm’s-eye view shows ordinary citizens squeezed by private corruption, public-sector failure, arbitrary regulation, and financial exclusion.

Banking rigidity drives the desperate to loan sharks

Financial literacy and inclusive banking also function poorly at ground level. Despite claims of wider outreach and sophisticated technology, formal institutions classify many small borrowers as non-bankable because they lack acceptable collateral, regular income records, or conventional credit histories. Yet these borrowers include traders and self-employed people whose livelihoods require small amounts of working capital. Commercial banks do little to build their capacity, monitor them closely, or bring them gradually into the formal system. When they urgently need funds to buy business stock, meet school expenses, or handle a medical emergency, they cannot wait through lengthy procedures. They are driven instead to informal moneylenders who ask few questions and provide cash immediately.

That convenience carries ruinous terms. Loans may have maturities as short as 100 days, with interest collected daily and amounting to as much as 10% a month. Daily collection makes each payment appear manageable, but the cumulative charge absorbs a large share of the borrower’s earnings. At maturity, the principal is commonly rolled over on the same terms because the borrower has been unable to save enough to repay it. A temporary cash shortage is thereby converted into perpetual debt, and income that should sustain a family or expand a microenterprise is transferred continuously to the lender.

The exploitation thrives in the absence of strict, modern usury laws and effective enforcement. Even the historic Ultra Duplum rule—which limits accumulated interest to the original principal—is bypassed or poorly enforced under the century-old Money Lending Ordinance and newer microfinance regulation to be enforced under the recently enacted Microfinance Regulatory Authority Act. Vulnerable borrowers rarely possess the knowledge, records, time, or resources needed to challenge abusive terms. The resulting anger is widespread in rural and urban communities. As the economics writer Yadamini Gunawardena observed by coining the term “The 5km Blind Spot”, such exploitation occurs within five kilometres of Colombo’s skyscraper-filled financial district—a systemic failure under policymakers’ noses. Financial inclusion cannot be measured only by the number of bank branches, accounts, or digital applications; it must also be judged by whether citizens can obtain safe, affordable credit when they need it.

Macroeconomic stability is essential, but it is not sufficient if people continue to experience insecurity, exploitation, and ineffective public services. This ‘not-so-rosy picture’ is the breeding ground for social, economic, and political disorders that will disable overnight, as happened in 2022, the much-praised stable and growing economy

Ground-level distress, a matter for concern

Taken together, these ground-level realities reveal a fractured recovery. The bird’s-eye view of lenders and policymakers shows fiscal discipline, single-digit inflation, rising reserves, and renewed growth. The worm’s-eye view shows ordinary citizens squeezed by private corruption, public-sector failure, arbitrary regulation, and financial exclusion. Macroeconomic stability is essential, but it is not sufficient if people continue to experience insecurity, exploitation, and ineffective public services. This ‘not-so-rosy picture’ is the breeding ground for social, economic, and political disorders that will disable overnight, as happened in 2022, the much-praised stable and growing economy.

(The writer, a former Deputy Governor of the Central bank of Sri Lanka, can be reached at waw1949@gmail.com )

title: Sri Lanka pay price of fifth bowler | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 2 November 2026 02:48
-     - 9

Pavan Rathnayake deserved to be Player of the Series

By Sa’adi Thawfeeq

Well, Sri Lanka lost the Pakistan ODI Tri-Series finale to the host country Pakistan. The result must have been rather disappointing for some, but no so for others who have been following the team’s progress in white ball cricket.

Not so long ago just two months back in September, Sri Lanka were thrashed 2-1 by England in the three-match ODI series. So inconsistent were their performances that sandwiched between a 16-run win at Headingley were two rather disappointing defeats in the first and third matches where Sri Lanka managed totals of just 176 and 132. It was exasperating to see the type of cricket they played, no fight back, but abject surrender.

Fast forward to October, it was a totally different Sri Lanka team we saw in the ODI Tri-Series. At the beginning of the tournament no one gave Sri Lanka a chance to even get closer to a final. It was to be a Pakistan-England final everyone was looking forward to.

But as the tournament progressed Sri Lanka began to gradually unveil their true potential. First it was that record run chase of 430 against England that would have lifted the spirits of the team sky high. It was then followed by the rout of Pakistan for 110 in the next match – a win that assured Sri Lanka a place in the final. There followed two back to back defeats against England in the final league match which was a dead rubber and in the final against Pakistan.

But what was most heartening from these results is that in three of their last four matches Sri Lanka topped 325 plus, which was something of an achievement if one was to look back on their performance in England. Mind you they scored these runs without one of their key top order batters Pathum Nissanka. After experimenting with several opening options Sri Lanka were successful with Kamindu Mendis and Avishka Fernando at the top. Each of them made over 200 runs in the tournament striking at 97.73 and 98.07 respectively. Kamindu Mendis went onto score a century in the final demonstrating his ability to play long innings and take responsibility, and Avishka recalled to the team after more than a year, missing out on a century by three runs against England in that record run chase.

If one was to critically analyse why Sri Lanka lost the final to Pakistan even after scoring 325 it was the absence of a fifth bowling option. Sri Lanka had Pakistan down at 14-2 and still allowed them to reach their target of 326. Fakhar Zaman’s splendid knock of 127 off 83 balls and Saad Baig’s contribution of 74 in a partnership of 149 changed the complexion of the chase.

Even after dismissing both batsmen and Salman Agha, Sri Lanka still couldn’t finish the job. Arafat Minhas produced a stunning counterattacking innings of 61 off just 31 deliveries, while Hasan Nawaz provided valuable support. That late partnership of 94 off 65 balls exposed Sri Lanka’s inability to control the game during the crucial overs. This is precisely where Sri Lanka’s lack of a fifth bowling option cost them the match. It wasn’t that Pakistan had an extraordinary batting lineup throughout the innings. Fakhar was exceptional, and Baig deserves credit for his contribution, but Sri Lanka gave away too many opportunities through their bowling, and crucial catches were spilled particularly when the pressure was on.

Against England, Sri Lanka’s fifth bowling option of Arachchige, Liyanage and Shanaka conceded 82 runs off nine overs, and against Pakistan 81 off 10. In the high scoring first match against England, Sri Lanka’s fifth bowling option of Shanaka, Kamindu Mendis and Liyanage leaked 123 runs off 10 overs, but it didn’t get highlighted because of Sri Lanka’s extraordinary run chase. Sri Lanka needs to address this important area before bigger tournaments. The lack of a genuine all-rounder is also a matter of concern.

On the positive side Sri Lanka has made vast strides especially in their batting. They’ll have to build their batting around Kamindu Mendis, Avishka Fernando, Pavan Rathnayake, and Janith Liyanage whose potential deserves backing.

The biggest positive is Pavan Rathnayake. What a tournament this 24-year-old cricketer from Mahanama College and CCC is having. Five innings, 427 runs, two centuries and two half-centuries, at an extraordinary average of 106.75. Beyond those numbers, what was most impressive was his resilience, patience, temperament and understanding of the game. His scores of 79 (74) against Pakistan, 130 (106) against England, 23* (26) against Pakistan, 118 (77) against England and 77 (65) in the final against Pakistan tell you the story of his consistency.

If ever a player deserved the Player of the Series award it was Rathnayake. His numbers tell the story. He was the highest run scorer of the tournament. No one came close! And yet the Player of the Series award goes to a player from the winning team. For all his brilliance on the field Rathnayake was presented with the All-Rounder of the Final and Best Fielder of the Final awards. Simply heartbreaking. Cricket is not just about who won the final, it›s about who dominated the whole series. And Rathnayake dominated it like no one else.

The one defeat in the final should not take away the appreciation the team deserves. The tournament demonstrated that Sri Lanka cricket had plenty of talent and character. The players deserve the encouragement, patience and unconditional support to attain greater heights.

title: End of an era: Soori and Hemakumari bow out as Sri Lanka Rugby Legends | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 2 November 2026 02:44
-     - 16

Srinath Sooriyabandara (centre) with (from left) SLR President Pavithra Fernando and Vice President Shanitha Fernando

Sandeeka Hemakumari (centre)

By Shamseer Jaleel

Sri Lanka Rugby paid tribute to two outstanding servants of the game, Srinath Sooriyabandara (Soori) and Sandeeka Hemakumari, as both brought the curtain down on remarkable international careers spanning 18 years each.

The two stalwarts were felicitated at a ceremony held at a leading hotel in Colombo recently by Sri Lanka Rugby, marking the end of distinguished careers that saw them serve Sri Lanka with commitment, passion and pride.

Sooriyabandara, who represented Sri Lanka from 2009 to 2026, began his career as a winger before legendary coach Hisham Abdeen converted him into a nippy and effective scrum-half. After making his mark at Isipathana College, Soori went on to represent CR & FC, Up-Country Lions and Kandy Sports Club.

A specialist in the sevens format, Soori represented Sri Lanka in both sevens and fifteens, while also earning the honour of captaining the national team. He was also the only Sri Lankan player selected to play in the Indian Rugby League alongside some of the world’s leading rugby players.

Following his retirement from international rugby, Soori is expected to return to his alma mater, Isipathana College, in a coaching capacity, opening a new chapter in his long association with the sport.

Hemakumari’s journey is equally inspiring, built on extraordinary commitment and sacrifice. Starting her rugby career in Avissawella, she regularly made four-hour return journeys to Colombo simply to attend training sessions.

A prolific sevens player, Hemakumari enjoyed an outstanding final club segment, scoring 22 tries to emerge as its leading try-scorer. Despite receiving lucrative offers to continue her career in Hong Kong and the UAE, she chose to remain committed to representing Sri Lanka.

Their retirement marks the end of an important chapter in Sri Lankan rugby, with Soori and Hemakumari leaving behind careers defined not only by their performances on the field but also by their dedication to the national jersey.

Sri Lanka Rugby’s felicitation served as a fitting tribute to two players who gave nearly two decades of their lives to the game and to their country.

title: Wushu makes its Olympic debut | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 2 November 2026 02:41
-     - 11

Wushu, also known popularly around the world as kungfu, is about to savour its Olympic debut as an official sport at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games.

Scores of wushu athletes around the globe have fallen in love with the centuries-old Chinese martial art by watching action movies with stars like Jet Li, Jackie Chan, Michelle Yeoh and Bruce Lee. The International Wushu Federation (IWUF), the governing body of wushu, has been steadily eyeing an Olympic dream since the sport’s founding in 1990. Formalizing centuries-old martial disciplines into a modern global sport that spans five continents has been no small task, but the 48 youth athletes representing 47 National Olympic Committee (NOCs) about to take the stage in Dakar are looking less back at history and more ahead to the shining Olympic medals to be won. 

Yet, these young athletes are keenly aware that they are making wushu and Olympic history. They can carve their names on this milestone that marks the first time that wushu has become an official competition sport at an Olympic event. Gold, silver and bronze medals will be awarded in four events:  Men’s Changquan Combined (Changquan and Gunshu), Women’s Changquan Combined (Changquan and Gunshu), Men’s’s Taijiqan Combined (Taijiquan and Taijishan), and Women’s Taijiquan Combined (Taijiquan and Taijishan). Young sports fans new to wushu will likely be dazzled by the artistry, power, dynamism, and daring athleticism of the athletes’ jumps, flips and weaponry. The subtle power and beauty of taiji will also be closely watched by some of the 150 million taiji fans worldwide. 

Dakar 2026 will be the first Olympic event ever held on the African continent. It is a historic milestone for the Olympic Movement and particularly significant for the new IOC President, Kirsty Coventry, a two-time Olympic swimming gold medalist from Zimbabwe, with South Africa also pursuing a bid to host the 2036 or 2040 Olympic Games

It is a fitting occasion for wushu to make its Olympic debut. The IWUF has placed considerable emphasis on developing wushu across Africa in recent years, with 43 National Federations now established across the continent. Reflecting this growth, young athletes from Senegal, Egypt, Rwanda, Morocco, Djibouti, Ethiopia, Niger, Gabon, Algeria, Tunisia and Benin have qualified for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games.

Athletes from the 47 NOCs have qualified for the Wushu Taolu competition at the Youth Olympic Games, Dakar 2026.

Leonard De Zilwa

Leonard De Zilwa, a former Sri Lankan national rugby player and accomplished coach with over two decades of experience in rugby development and high-performance coaching, will be taking charge as the Head Coach of the youthful CH and FC outfit at the Inter Club League rugby tournament 2026/2027.

Representing Sri Lanka from 1992 to 2002, Leonard was the first Captain of Sri Lanka’s rugby sevens team at the 2002 Commonwealth Games in Manchester, when rugby 7s made its debut at the Games.

He also captained the national team at the Hong Kong 7s and Dubai International 7s and was part of the Asian Quadrangular Championship-winning team in 1997.

As a coach, De Zilwa has guided MAS Holdings to four Mercantile Rugby Championship titles and Navy SC to the 2013/14 A Division Club Championship. His coaching career includes serving as Head Coach of the Sri Lanka Women’s Rugby 7s Team at the 2026 CASA Rugby Sevens, alongside coaching appointments at Ananda College, St. Peter’s College, St. Thomas’ College and John Paul College, New Zealand.

Former Secretary, CH and FC, Shane Dulawewa and former leading referee, Tony Amit, are giving the Maitland Crescent club a big hand in setting up a young unit this season. (SJ)

title: Beyond cricket: How franchise sports are reshaping Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 2 November 2026 00:56
-     - 8

By Chantal Perera

The expansion of franchise-based competitions beyond cricket is opening new opportunities for athletes, brands and investors, with the Sri Lanka Padel League helping pioneer a new era for the country’s sporting industry.

For decades, cricket dominated Sri Lanka’s sporting landscape, attracting the majority of commercial investment and sponsorship. However, the emergence of franchise-based competitions across multiple sports is beginning to change that picture, creating new opportunities for athletes, businesses and sporting organisations.

Sri Lanka’s franchise-sports journey began with the Sri Lanka Premier League (SLPL) cricket initiative in 2012. Following its failure to establish a sustainable competition, the Lanka Premier League (LPL) was launched in 2020, bringing renewed attention to the commercial potential of the franchise model.

The next significant step came with the expansion of franchise sports beyond cricket. The Sri Lanka Padel League helped pioneer this new chapter, demonstrating that the franchise model could extend beyond cricket and opening the door for a wider range of sporting properties to emerge. The Ceylon Golf League followed, with franchise-based competitions subsequently expanding into pickleball, tennis, rugby and rowing. A franchise-based archery league has also joined this growing landscape.

Together, these developments signal the emergence of a broader sports-business ecosystem in Sri Lanka, extending the franchise model into an increasingly diverse range of disciplines.

For athletes, franchise leagues can provide greater visibility, more competitive opportunities and potential income through participation and sponsorships. They can also create platforms for talent development, professional exposure and stronger connections with sporting audiences.

High-quality live broadcasting and production have become another important pillar of this evolution. From live match coverage to televised player auctions, these productions bring audiences closer to the competition, allowing fans to follow team formations, player selections and the sporting action itself. They also give sponsors greater visibility through broadcast integrations, on-screen branding and digital content, extending commercial exposure beyond the physical venue. By presenting these competitions as professionally produced sporting entertainment, leagues can attract wider audiences and strengthen their appeal to commercial partners.

The commercial opportunities are equally significant. Brands that have traditionally focused on cricket can now explore partnerships across golf, padel, pickleball, tennis, rugby, rowing and archery. These leagues offer opportunities for targeted sponsorships, digital exposure, hospitality and experiential marketing, enabling businesses to connect with new audiences and sporting communities.

The movement also creates opportunities for broadcasters, technology providers, event organisers and sports marketing professionals, while encouraging private investment in the development of sporting properties.

Long-term success will depend on sustainable finances, consistent competition, strong commercial partnerships and the ability to deliver value to athletes, sponsors and franchise owners. Nevertheless, the growing diversity of leagues demonstrates that franchise-based sport is becoming an increasingly important part of Sri Lanka’s sporting landscape.

What was once largely associated with cricket is now creating opportunities across multiple disciplines. With the Sri Lanka Padel League helping lead the expansion beyond cricket, the country is entering a new chapter in which franchise sports can contribute to athlete development, commercial investment and the wider growth of the sports industry.

title: NSSF sends 11 athletes for ISSF World Championship in Doha | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 2 November 2026 00:55
-     - 7

Sri Lanka will send 11 of its finest marksmen and markswomen for the ISSF (International Shooting Sport Federation) World Championship 2026 to be held in Doha, Qatar from 1 to 14 November. The team will include seven female shooters and four male shooters, who will collectively compete under seven different categories with the expectation of performing impressively at the event.

The ISSF World Championship is the first Olympic Quota Qualification Competition, with over 1,000 athletes representing 90 countries trying to break into the Los Angeles Olympic Games 2028. The final selection was confirmed by the National Shooting Sport Federation of Sri Lanka (NSSF) earlier this week.

The participating athletes are Siyathi Disakya Galagedara, Umaya Akarshani Kumarasiri, Nehasha Weerasinghe, Reinya Ranasinghe, Amali Kulathunge, Ruwini Abeymanna and Dinushi Rajapaksha, all female, and male shooters Kumarathunga Herath, Sameera Ranganath, Kaushan Muditha Samaranayake and Beverly Gavin Jayasekara.

Siyathi Galagedara, Umaya Kumarasiri and Nehasha Weerasinghe will compete in the 10m Air Pistol Women event, while Reinya Ranasinghe, Amali Kulathunge and Ruwini Abeymanna will feature in both the 25m Sport Pistol Women and 25m Standard Pistol Women events. The remaining female athlete, Dinushi Rajapaksha, will compete in the 50m 3x20 Rifle Women event. Among the four competing men, Herath will compete in the 25m Standard Pistol Men event, while Ranganath tries his fortune in the 50m 3x20 Rifle Men event. Clay target shooters Samaranayake and Jayasekara will compete in the Trap event, which is scheduled during the latter stages of the competition.

The team will be assisted by four officials, including Dinesh Lionel as the Team Manager, Sagara Wimaladharma as the Team Coach, Nivantha Waas as Official for the Trap Event and Nalinda Ranasinghe as Official for other events. The team will leave for Doha in separate batches in accordance with their respective event schedules.

Athletes: Siyathi Disakya Galagedara (10m Air Rifle Women/House of Shooting SAC), Umaya Akarshani Kumarasiri (10m Air Rifle Women/Clay Target Shooting Club of Colombo), Nehasha Weerasinghe (10m Air Pistol Women/Cambrian Shooting SC), Reinya Ranasinghe (25m Sport Pistol Women, 25m Standard Pistol Women/Hill Country SSC), Amali Kulathunge (25m Sport Pistol Women, 25m Standard Pistol Women/Cambrian Shooting SC), Ruwini Abeymanna (25m Sport Pistol Women, 25m Standard Pistol Women/Negombo Rifle Club), Dinushi Rajapaksha (50m 3x20 Rifle Women/Sri Lanka Air Force SC), Kumarathunga Herath (25m Standard Pistol Men/Army Small Arms Association), Sameera Ranganath (50m 3x20 Rifle Men/Sri Lanka Navy Musketry), Kaushan Muditha Samaranayake (Trap/Negombo Rifle Club), Beverly Gavin Jayasekara (Trap/Clay Target Shooting Club of Colombo).

Officials: Dinesh Lionel (Team Manager), Sagara Wimaladharma (Team Coach), Nivantha Waas (Official, Trap Event), Nalinda Ranasinghe (Official).

Omega Line Sports Club delivered an outstanding performance at two of Sri Lanka’s major corporate sporting events, securing three championship titles and a runner-up finish at the 2026 Mercantile Netball Knockout Tournament and the Mercantile Volleyball Championship.

At the Mercantile Netball Knockout Tournament, which concluded recently on the 11th at the Air Force Indoor Sports Complex in Thummulla, Omega Line Women’s B Team emerged champions of the ‘C’ Division, securing first place in the category.

CDB Bank scored 47 points, while Omega Line A accumulated 39 points. This achievement marked a significant milestone in the history of Omega Line Mercantile Netball, as it was the first time Omega Line Sports Club had achieved such a result while competing in the ‘A’ Division.

The Mercantile Volleyball Championship also concluded recently at the indoor stadium of Dhammissara College in Nattandiya, where Omega Line’s women’s teams delivered another series of impressive performances.

In the Women’s Championship Division final, Omega Line defeated United Tobacco in straight sets, winning 3-0 to claim the championship title.

Omega Line continued its winning streak in the ‘A’ Division final, where the women’s team secured another championship title with a convincing 3-0 victory over Aqua Dynamics.

The Women’s Super League final proved to be a highly competitive encounter between Omega Line Sports Club and the Hydramani team. Following an intense contest, Omega Line secured the runner-up position in the category.

Omega Line Sports Club’s exceptional performances and impressive collection of victories throughout the tournaments earned widespread recognition. The team demonstrated outstanding skill, determination and sportsmanship while competing against strong teams representing some of the country’s leading corporate organisations.

Representing a group of affiliated companies in Sri Lanka’s apparel industry, Omega Line Sports Club participated in the 2026 Mercantile Netball and Volleyball tournaments on behalf of the group comprising Sirio Ltd, Alpha Apparels, Benji and Omega Line. title: Man United on brink of Premier League relegation zone | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 2 November 2026 00:54
-     - 5

Coventry City manager Frank Lampard celebrates after the Sunderland match

Joint record Premier League winners Manchester United were plunged to the brink of the relegation zone by their defeat at Chelsea followed by Coventry City’s win against Sunderland.

Ten-man United were beaten 2-0 at Stamford Bridge in the early kickoff in the English top flight, leaving them on their first nine-match winless run since 1986. The Red Devils have already made their worst start to a league season in 40 years.

Despite an improved display in the first-half, in which recalled captain Bruno Fernandes spurned one of many key chances, United were beaten by a brilliant solo goal by Morgan Rogers and a penalty converted by Cole Palmer.

Lisandro Martinez was shown a second yellow card for a reckless challenge on Wesley Fofana in an aerial duel from a corner. United’s day was about to get worse. Coventry City’s 3-1 home win against Sunderland saw them leapfrog the fallen giants, leaving United just one point and one place outside the relegation zone.

There’s a chance the 20-time English champions, who have won only once in nine league games, could be in the bottom three by the end of Matchweek 9 – a desperate situation for a club widely regarded as the biggest in the country.

Man United’s only two victories from 13 matches in all competitions this season were against promoted Ipswich in the Premier League and tournament newcomer Sabah in the Champions League.

United’s next match is at home to Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday with yet more doubts on whether Carrick will still be in charge.

Only Nottingham Forest’s 2-0 defeat at Brentford ensured United did not drop into the bottom three.

The pressure is piling onto Carrick, who is only in his first full season in charge.

The former midfielder remains in defiant mood.

“The two halves of football couldn’t probably be further apart,” said Carrick, who added he expects to be in charge for Tuesday’s Champions League tie against Roma.

“We looked in a good place going into half-time and then found a way of unravelling it second half.”

A point for Crystal Palace in the final Premier League game of the day at Tottenham will see United fall into the bottom three.

Pelwatte’s support of the team reflects its broader commitment to creating opportunities for Sri Lankan youth to participate in sports and extracurricular activities that contribute to their personal development.
